sites.se: Seven layers of a capital, from Dilmun to the Portuguese
sites.sa: سبع طبقات لعاصمة، من دلمون إلى البرتغاليين
sites.desc: A 12 m high tell on the north coast, 6 km from Manama, with seven stratified occupation layers from about 2300 BC to the 16th century AD. Regarded as the capital of Dilmun, it holds a Dilmun palace with warehouses, a Kassite palace, residential quarters on 12 m wide streets, city walls and gates, and the Portuguese fort on top that gave the site its name. About 25% of the 17.5 ha site has been excavated. Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2005.
sites.sig: The longest continuous archaeological sequence in the Gulf and the only Dilmun-period city excavated at scale. About 50 cuneiform tablets were found, three from the reign of the Kassite king Agum.

sites.se: Three temples built over a sacred spring to the god of fresh water
sites.sa: ثلاثة معابد بُنيت فوق عين مقدسة لإله الماء العذب
sites.desc: Three temples built one above the other at the village of Barbar. Temple I (c. 3000 BC) stood on a platform about 25 by 16–18 m of local stone; Temple II, about 500 years later, enlarged the terrace in limestone; Temple III (2100–2000 BC) was the largest and stayed in use into the early 2nd millennium BC. A natural spring filled a pool in a subterranean shrine, read as the abzu of Enki, god of wisdom and fresh water, with channels carrying water to fields and gardens. Limestone blocks are thought to have been quarried on Jidda Island and brought by boat.
sites.sig: The clearest expression of Dilmun's water cult and one of the oldest temple sequences in the Gulf. The copper bull's head from Temple II is the emblem of the Bahrain National Museum.

sites.te: A town that kept its seals
sites.se: Several hundred stamp seals from the houses of one small Dilmun town
sites.sa: مئات الأختام من بيوت بلدة دلمونية صغيرة
sites.desc: A planned Early Dilmun town of about 2.5 ha west of Manama, with houses along streets and a temple believed to have marked the summer solstice. Found in a 1977 survey and excavated 1977–1979 under M. Ibrahim, then by the London–Bahrain Archaeological Expedition in 1990–1999. Finds include copper fishhooks, bitumen imported from Mesopotamia, pearl-oyster shell and seed pearls, and several hundred stamp seals, four or five in a single house; 48 more came from the adjoining burial ground.
sites.sig: The most complete plan of an ordinary Dilmun town and the richest seal assemblage from domestic contexts anywhere in the Gulf.

sites.te: The well that was a temple
sites.se: Stone-built wells at a spring, treated as holy places
sites.sa: آبار مبنية بالحجر عند عين، عوملت كأماكن مقدسة
sites.desc: A spring site in Diraz whose name means 'mother of the spring of overflowing waters'. An oval hollow about 60 by 30 m holds stone-built wells dated to the 3rd millennium BC, with rooms and ovens added later on the south side. First dug by the Danish expedition in 1954; a Rikkyo University (Japan) team in the 1990s identified three wells and was the first to interpret them as holy places. The northern well is known as the water temple.
sites.sig: Links the Dilmun water cult of Barbar to the island's spring line; one of the few shrines built directly on a spring.

sites.te: Where the kings of Dilmun lie
sites.se: Seventeen giant mounds in one village, the tombs of Dilmun’s first kings
sites.sa: سبعة عشر تلًا عملاقًا في قرية واحدة، مدافن أوائل ملوك دلمون
sites.desc: Seventeen royal mounds (13 single and two pairs) in the village of A'ali, up to 50 m in diameter and 12 m high, built between about 2050 and 1750 BC when Dilmun was ruled by kings. Chieftain mounds of 13–26 m lie around them. Three cuneiform inscriptions were found in Mound 8. The royal mounds form 15 of the 21 components of the Dilmun Burial Mounds World Heritage property inscribed in 2019.
sites.sig: The earliest monumental royal tombs in Eastern Arabia and the main evidence for the emergence of kingship in Dilmun.

sites.n: Hamad Town and Janabiyah Mound Fields
sites.s: Dilmun burial mound fields · World Heritage
sites.el: Fields of some dozen to several thousand tumuli
sites.se: Tens of thousands of small mounds once covered the north of the island
sites.sa: عشرات الآلاف من التلال الصغيرة غطّت يومًا شمال الجزيرة
sites.desc: Mound fields west and south of A'ali that make up six of the 21 components of the Dilmun Burial Mounds property, about 11,774 mounds in all. Early Type mounds (c. 2200–2050 BC) average 2.5 m across and under 1.5 m high; about 1,000 survive of an estimated 17,000. Late Type mounds (c. 2050–1750 BC) are 6–11 m across and 2–3 m high; mapping suggested 58,000 once existed, with about 13,500 remaining. Each mound covers a central stone chamber inside a low ring wall; Janabiyah and Madinat Hamad 2 hold mounds with subsidiary burials.
sites.sig: One of the densest Bronze Age cemetery landscapes known anywhere, and a record of how a whole island population buried its dead for four centuries.

sites.se: Ninety graves in one mound, and the ashes of funeral banquets
sites.sa: تسعون قبرًا في تل واحد، ورماد ولائم الجنازة
sites.desc: A burial mound about 80 m long in the village of Shakhura, used from the 3rd century BC to the 4th century AD, when Bahrain was known as Tylos. Excavations led by Captain Robert Higham in the 1960s found 90 graves, the earliest at the centre and later ones added in arcs, with Roman and Parthian artefacts including an intact ribbed glass bowl now in the British Museum. A 2008 excavation found an ash layer with glazed pottery, fish and animal bones, read as the remains of funeral banquets. The mound was largely demolished in the 1990s.
sites.sig: A key site for the Tylos period, when the island traded with the Hellenistic and Parthian worlds.

sites.s: Early Islamic mosque with twin minarets
sites.se: The oldest standing mosque in Bahrain, rebuilt twice
sites.sa: أقدم مسجد قائم في البحرين، أُعيد بناؤه مرتين
sites.desc: Traditionally founded in 692 AD, but an inscription points to an 11th-century foundation under the Uyunids, when it had one minaret; the second minaret was added about two centuries later under the Usfurids. The mosque was rebuilt in the 14th and 15th centuries: an early prayer hall with a flat roof on wooden columns, and a later section on arches and masonry piers dated to 1339. A 12th-century limestone mihrab slab carrying Qur'anic verses was found during restoration. Recent excavations by the Early Islamic Bahrain Project place it within Bilad al-Qadim, the main centre of settlement in the 11th–13th centuries.
sites.sig: The principal surviving monument of medieval Bahrain and the anchor of the Bilad al-Qadim heritage trail.

sites.se: The main town of the island when Manama did not yet exist
sites.sa: البلدة الرئيسية في الجزيرة قبل أن توجد المنامة
sites.desc: An area of Islamic-period settlement in the north-east of the main island, the main centre of settlement in the 11th–13th centuries AD, named 'the old town' after Manama grew beside it. Excavations by the Anglo-Bahraini Early Islamic Bahrain Project at the Al-Khamis Mosque, the spring of Ain Abu Zaydan and the Abu Anbra cemetery have traced houses, water systems and burials of the medieval town.
sites.sig: The only medieval Islamic town in the Gulf islands studied over two decades of excavation; a bridge between Dilmun-era springs and the modern capital.

sites.el: Square plan with four round towers
sites.te: The fort on its own island
sites.se: A square fort that once stood on an islet, now joined to Muharraq
sites.sa: قلعة مربعة كانت على جزيرة صغيرة، التحمت اليوم بالمحرق
sites.desc: A square fort with a cylindrical tower at each corner, built in the late 15th or early 16th century, before the Portuguese occupation of 1622; a Portuguese map of about 1635 shows it under siege with inner and outer walls. A trench once filled from wells surrounded it, and nose-shaped openings for marksmen pierce the upper walls. Restored in 1984–1987 under architect Archie Walls using sea stone, lime, sand and palm trunks, without cement. The fort stood on a separate islet before land reclamation joined it to Muharraq.
sites.sig: The best-preserved Islamic-period fort in Bahrain and a model restoration in traditional materials.

sites.el: On the cliff over the Hunanaiya valley
sites.se: Rebuilt in 1812 on an older foundation, home of the ruling family
sites.sa: أُعيد بناؤها عام 1812 على أساس أقدم، وكانت مسكن الأسرة الحاكمة
sites.desc: A fort on the cliff between East and West Riffa, first built in the early 18th century by Fareer bin Rahhal and rebuilt on its foundations in 1812–1818 by Sheikh Salman bin Ahmed Al Fateh Al Khalifa, who used it as a residence. Sheikh Isa bin Ali Al Khalifa, ruler from 1869 to 1932, was born here. The fort was restored in 1993 and overlooks the desert valley cut into the island's interior escarpment.
sites.sig: Marks the move of the ruling family's seat inland in the early 19th century and sits on the island's geological rim.

sites.n: Pearling Path and Bu Maher Fort
sites.te: The road to the oyster beds
sites.se: Seventeen houses, a fort and three oyster beds that made an island economy
sites.sa: سبعة عشر بيتًا وقلعة وثلاث مغاصات صنعت اقتصاد جزيرة
sites.desc: A 3.5 km path through Muharraq linking 17 historic buildings, from the seafront Bu Maher fort on the island's southern tip to the Siyadi complex, together with three oyster beds in the northern waters. Pearl diving in the Gulf is mentioned in Assyrian texts of about 2000 BC; the economy that these buildings record ran from the 2nd century to the 1930s, with a golden age from the 1850s to 1930, before oil was found in 1932 and cultured pearls ended the trade. Inscribed on the World Heritage List on 30 June 2012.
sites.sig: The last complete example of the cultural tradition of pearling that shaped the Gulf for two millennia.

sites.se: The highest point of a slow dome of Eocene limestone
sites.sa: أعلى نقطة في قبة بطيئة من حجر الإيوسين الجيري
sites.desc: The island's highest point at 134.1 m, near its geographic centre, on the axis of the north–south Bahrain anticline. The fold is simple, with no surface faults; subsurface faults are normal tension faults with throws usually under 15 m. The core exposes the lower Eocene Rus Formation (about 67 m thick, chalky dolomitic limestone with chert and anhydrite), overlain by the Dammam Formation, whose rimrock of Eocene limestone encircles the central basin in cliffs more than 30 m high. Bahrain's first oil well was drilled at its foot in 1932.
sites.sig: The structural heart of Bahrain: the anticline that traps the island's oil and gas and lifts its oldest rocks to the surface.

sites.n: First Oil Well and the Bahrain Field
sites.te: Where the Gulf’s oil age began
sites.ta: حيث بدأ عصر النفط في الخليج
sites.se: Oil first spurted below Jebel Dukhan on 16 October 1931
sites.sa: تدفق النفط أول مرة أسفل جبل الدخان في 16 أكتوبر 1931
sites.desc: Well No. 1 below Jebel Dukhan, where oil first spurted on 16 October 1931 and flowed from 2 June 1932: the first oil found on the Arabian side of the Gulf. Frank Holmes had won a concession in 1925 after first finding fresh water for the ruler; the Bahrain Petroleum Company (Bapco) was set up in 1929 by Standard Oil of California. The Awali (now Bahrain) field covers about 400 km², roughly 80% of the main island, with oil reservoirs between 380 and 2,000 m and gas to nearly 4,000 m. Output peaked at about 80,000 barrels a day in 1971; gas was found in 1948 and the offshore Abu Safah field in 1963.
sites.sig: The discovery that started the Gulf oil industry, drilled on the anticline that geology had already revealed at the surface.

sites.te: The bowl in the middle of the island
sites.se: A ring of limestone cliffs around a hollow where the dome was eaten away
sites.sa: حلقة من الجروف الجيرية حول تجويف أُكلت فيه القبة
sites.desc: A closed basin in the centre of the island, ringed by a rimrock of Eocene Dammam limestone standing in cliffs more than 30 m high. Erosion cut through the crest of the Bahrain anticline, removing the younger beds and exposing the Rus Formation inside the ring; the basin is the only place with meaningful local recharge of groundwater. The Dammam Formation has four members here: the 'shark's-tooth shale' (9–15 m), a brown crystalline limestone (about 33 m), an orange marl (6–20 m) and a white limestone (6–62 m).
sites.sig: A textbook breached anticline, and the landscape that explains Bahrain's springs, quarries and oil in one view.

sites.s: Fossil bed of the Dammam Formation
sites.se: A grey shale full of shark teeth, laid down when Bahrain was sea floor
sites.sa: طفل رمادي مليء بأسنان القرش، ترسّب حين كانت البحرين قاع بحر
sites.desc: The lowest member of the Dammam Formation on Bahrain: 9.1–15.2 m of grey to yellow shale and marl named for its abundant fossil shark teeth, exposed on the inner slopes of the rimrock. It records the shallow Eocene sea that covered the region about 50 million years ago, before the Tertiary limestones were uplifted on the anticline.
sites.sig: The island's most accessible fossil bed and a marker horizon used to map the whole Dammam Formation across eastern Arabia.

sites.s: Artesian springs of the land of two seas
sites.se: Fresh water from Saudi Arabia rises through the island’s limestone
sites.sa: ماء عذب من السعودية يصعد عبر حجر الجزيرة الجيري
sites.desc: Bahrain's springs rise from the Dammam Formation's Khobar and Alat limestones, recharged where the beds outcrop in Saudi Arabia; the Khobar member supplies over 75% of groundwater. Ain Adhari, south-west of Manama, was described as a river of fast water about three metres wide feeding the date groves. Abstraction from the Dammam rose from about 63 million m³ in 1952 to 188 million m³ in 2001, about 68% above the estimated inflow of 112 million m³, and the saline front advanced 60–139 m a year; most springs, including Adhari, no longer flow naturally and almost 70% of usable groundwater has been lost or salinised.
sites.sig: The hydrogeology behind Dilmun's temples, the medieval towns and the island's name, and a warning written in salt.

sites.se: Divers filled goatskins from springs on the sea bed, especially off Muharraq
sites.sa: غاصوا ليملأوا القِرب من عيون في قاع البحر، خصوصًا قبالة المحرق
sites.desc: Fresh water from the same Eocene aquifer that feeds the land springs also rises through the sea floor around the islands, most numerously off Muharraq. An 1829 British traveller described a spring in about three fathoms of water; divers fitted a jar over the spring mouth and filled goatskin bags, and pearling crews used the springs to take on water at sea. The phenomenon is the origin of the name 'Bahrain', the two seas of salt and sweet water. Location shown is approximate.

sites.s: Coastal salt flats of the south
sites.te: Where the island turns to salt
sites.se: Beach sands and salt crusts on the island’s quiet southern tip
sites.sa: رمال شاطئية وقشور ملح على طرف الجزيرة الجنوبي الهادئ
sites.desc: Recent beach sands and sabkha (salt-flat) deposits concentrated at Ra's al Jaza'ir and Ra's al Barr in the south and south-west of the island, where the land is low and the Eocene aquifers carry water too saline for use. The sabkha surface forms as sea water and brine evaporate in the capillary zone, leaving gypsum and halite crusts; the sand gazelle and migrating waders use the surrounding flats.
sites.sig: The modern end of Bahrain's story: evaporite forming today on the same island whose Eocene rocks hold anhydrite from an older sea.

sites.te: Islands of a hundred thousand birds
sites.se: The world’s largest breeding colony of Socotra cormorants, with dugongs and gazelles
sites.sa: أكبر مستعمرة تكاثر لغراب البحر السوقطري في العالم، مع الأطوم والغزلان
sites.desc: An archipelago of 16 main desert islands (36 in all) about 19 km south-east of the main island, with a highest point of 22 m; Hawar itself is over 41 km². Designated a Ramsar wetland of 5,200 ha on 27 October 1997 and a national protected area with access restricted by the coast guard. In 1992, 200,000–300,000 adult Socotra cormorants were recorded, the largest known breeding concentration in the world; greater flamingos and gulls winter in numbers, dugongs and sea turtles feed on the seagrass beds, and reintroduced Arabian oryx and sand gazelle live on the main island.
sites.sig: One of the most important seabird sites in the Middle East and the only part of Bahrain in near-pristine condition.

sites.n: Tubli Bay and Ras Sanad Mangroves
sites.se: A shrinking bay that still feeds thousands of wintering shorebirds
sites.sa: خليج يتقلص لكنه ما زال يطعم آلاف الطيور الشاطئية الشاتية
sites.desc: A shallow bay of 1,350 ha between Manama and Sitra, protected by Royal Decree in 2006 and listed as a Ramsar wetland. The Avicennia marina stand at Ras Sanad in its south-west corner is Bahrain's last natural mangrove and a wildlife reserve. It is the country's most important site for migrating and wintering waterbirds, with counts of 2,000 black-headed gulls, 1,000 little stints, 300 ringed plovers and 250 ruddy turnstones. Since 1975 most of the original mangrove, intertidal and date-palm habitats have been lost to reclamation, roads and sewage, especially on the northern shore.
sites.sig: A living remnant of the mangrove coast that once lined the island, and a measure of what reclamation costs.

sites.n: Al Areen Wildlife Park and Reserve
sites.se: A fenced reserve that bred the Arabian oryx and gazelle for release on Hawar
sites.sa: محمية مسيّجة ربّت المها العربي والغزال لإطلاقهما في حوار
sites.desc: A fenced desert reserve of about 8 km² at Sakhir on the west side of the island, founded in 1976 and divided into a public park and a protected reserve with two surface reservoirs. It holds indigenous plants and animals plus exotic species from Africa and Asia, with 82 bird species and more than 45 animal species recorded; its flagship animals are the Arabian oryx, once extinct in the wild, and the reem (sand) gazelle. Oryx and gazelle bred here were reintroduced to the Hawar Islands.

sites.te: A reef at the edge of endurance
sites.se: Corals here survive 37 °C summers, then lose almost everything in a bad year
sites.sa: تصمد الشعاب هنا أمام صيف بحرارة 37 درجة، ثم تخسر كل شيء تقريبًا في سنة سيئة
sites.desc: A reef platform of about 200 km² east of the main island; Bahrain's reef areas (fashts) total about 850 km², more than its land area. In the 1980s about 30 coral species were recorded, with Acropora cover of 50–90% in 1988; mass bleaching in 1996 (37.7 °C) and 1998 (38 °C) hit Bahrain harder than any other Gulf country, and the 2017 event, above 34 °C from July to October, cut nearshore hard-coral cover from 13.6% to 1.4%. The survivors are massive Platygyra, Favia and Porites; branching corals are essentially gone, and the nearshore carbonate budget has fallen to near zero.
sites.sig: Among the world's most heat-tolerant reefs, and a front line of climate change in the Gulf.

sites.n: Dugongs of the Gulf of Salwa
sites.te: The sea cows of the shallows
sites.se: Herds of several hundred dugongs graze the seagrass between Bahrain and Qatar
sites.sa: قطعان من مئات الأطوم ترعى الأعشاب البحرية بين البحرين وقطر
sites.desc: The shallow waters south of Bahrain, mostly under 10 m deep with extensive Halodule and Halophila seagrass, hold the world's second-largest dugong population after Australia. A herd of 674 was counted in March 1986, with calves 15.7% of the group; winter surveys in 2004 recorded groups of 577 and 97 between Bahrain and Qatar, and 508 animals were counted in under 1 km² in 2015–2016. Bahrain surveys in 2006 gave estimates similar to those of twenty years earlier. The area is an Important Marine Mammal Area of 10,676 km² that also holds humpback and bottlenose dolphins and finless porpoises.
sites.sig: A globally important population of a vulnerable species, dependent on the same seagrass that feeds Hawar's turtles.

sites.s: Lone mesquite in the southern desert
sites.el: 9.75 m tall · 6 km from Jebel Dukhan
sites.se: A 400-year-old tree alive in bare desert, its water still unexplained
sites.sa: شجرة عمرها 400 عام حيّة في صحراء جرداء، وماؤها ما زال لغزًا
sites.desc: A Prosopis (mesquite) tree 9.75 m tall standing alone on a low hill about 6 km from Jebel Dukhan and 40 km from Manama. A 1990s soil and tree-ring study dated its planting to 1582. Its roots may reach 50 m down to groundwater, though no spring is visible; other explanations invoke moisture held in the sand. Archaeologists in October 2010 unearthed 500-year-old pottery and other artefacts beside it, and about 65,000 people visit each year.
sites.sig: A living test of the island's hidden water, and the most visited natural site in Bahrain.

sites.se: A columned Dilmun temple beside the Budaiya Highway, unlike anything at Barbar or in Mesopotamia
sites.sa: معبد دلموني ذو أعمدة قرب طريق البديع، لا يشبه معبد باربار ولا معابد بلاد الرافدين
sites.desc: Only about 700 m² survive, in the south-western corner of an original settlement just north of the Budaiya Highway in Diraz. A central hall held two rows of cylindrical columns about 120 cm in diameter, of which nine remain standing up to 60 cm high, spaced 2 to 3 m apart, with a square base between them read as an altar or statue base and a small square cella to the east. A British expedition partly explored the site in 1973–75 with the Bahrain Directorate of Archaeology, finding Barbar-type pottery, a snake vessel and two Dilmun stamp seals with animal figures; the finds date it to the 3rd or early 2nd millennium BC. East of the temple a subterranean tomb of the Kassite period stayed in use into the Iron Age.
sites.sig: Its column architecture differs from both Mesopotamian temples and the nearby Barbar temple, so it records a separate strand of Dilmun religious building.

sites.s: Late Stone Age fishing camp · Ubaid pottery
sites.se: A sand-covered mound in the south-west where Stone Age fishers left painted Ubaid sherds and thousands of flints
sites.sa: تل مغطى بالرمل في الجنوب الغربي ترك فيه صيادو العصر الحجري كسر فخار عبيدي ملوّن وآلاف الأدوات الصوانية
sites.desc: A low, sand-covered mound about 6 km south of Zallaq and 1,200 m from the present shore. Ubaid-period sherds were noticed in 1971 and a British team under Michael Roaf excavated it in 1975, recovering 6,896 flint pieces, mainly scrapers, with pottery dated to about 3800 BC. The earlier phase holds painted late or post-Ubaid sherds that were mended and reused, bones of sparid fish, pearl oyster and other shellfish, and shallow fire pits; the later phase has little pottery, more flint, larger fish, and the first bones of goat, hare and dugong, which were common. Sea level in the late Neolithic is thought to have stood up to 4 m higher, so the mound may once have been an islet used seasonally by fishers and hunters.
sites.sig: The main Ubaid-related site in Bahrain and one of the earliest records of dugong hunting in the Gulf.

sites.s: Earliest Dilmun cairn graveyard · Japanese excavations
sites.el: Wadi 4 km long · hundreds of mounds
sites.se: Hundreds of early cairn mounds along a wadi on the plateau, radiocarbon-dated to about 2300 BC
sites.sa: مئات المدافن الركامية المبكرة على جانبي وادٍ في الهضبة، مؤرخة بالكربون المشع إلى نحو 2300 قبل الميلاد
sites.desc: A wadi about 4 km long on the inland plateau, running from south-east to north-west, with hundreds of 'Riffa type' burial mounds along its slopes, mainly in the upper 3 km; mounds of this type were once scattered around Riffa but were mostly lost to building, so those in the wadi are the survivors. A Kanazawa University mission led by Takeshi Gotoh excavated 15 mounds in the northern part over five seasons from 2015 to 2019, while the Bahrain Authority for Culture and Antiquities dug 11 more; 266 possible mounds were identified there. All were cairn burials, and eight radiocarbon dates fall between 2300 and 1900 BC, so construction probably began around 2300 BC or earlier. Some graves held Mesopotamian and Umm an-Nar pottery and stone beads, evidence of maritime trade by the end of the 3rd millennium BC.
sites.sig: The earliest phase of the Dilmun mound tradition, showing the rise of a tribal society before the royal mounds of A'ali.

sites.el: Four phases of use over two millennia
sites.se: Underground rock-cut tombs reused from Dilmun to Tylos times, where the first Dilmun seal in a grave was found
sites.sa: مدافن منحوتة تحت الأرض أُعيد استخدامها من دلمون إلى تايلوس، وفيها وُجد أول ختم دلموني داخل قبر
sites.desc: A cemetery on the edge of the Budaiya Highway at the village of Al-Hajjar, explored mainly by the Bahrain Department of Antiquities in 1970–71 and again in the mid-1990s. Its northern complex of underground rock-cut graves, some still sealed with flat capstones, is rare in Bahrain; it was used in the Early Dilmun period (c. 2000–1800 BC), under the Kassites (c. 1400–1300 BC), in Late Dilmun times (c. 900–800 BC) and in the Tylos period (c. 200 BC – 300 AD), and the southern part holds unexcavated Tylos mounds. In 1970 the first Early Dilmun stamp seal ever found in a grave was recovered near a skeleton's neck. Later offerings include soft-stone and alabaster vessels, stamp and cylinder seals, glass, iron weapons, jewellery and two limestone statues unique in Bahrain, now in the Bahrain National Museum.
sites.sig: The clearest case in Bahrain of one burial ground reused across four cultural periods, from Dilmun to the Hellenistic-Parthian world.

sites.te: Dice from the age of Tylos
sites.se: A circular burial hill 8 km west of Manama with nearly a hundred built graves of the Tylos age
sites.sa: تل مدافن دائري على بعد 8 كم غرب المنامة فيه نحو مئة قبر مبني من عصر تايلوس
sites.desc: A circular mound about 70 m across and 4 to 4.5 m high, 8 km west of Manama and 500 m south of the Janusan roundabout on the Budaiya road. A Bahraini team dug briefly in 1983, finding glazed pottery, glass, jewellery and tombstones now in the Tylos hall of the Bahrain National Museum; since 2017 the French Archaeological Mission under Pierre Lombard has worked with the Bahrain Authority for Culture and Antiquities. By 2021 nearly 70 built graves including three burial jars had been revealed over about 1,000 m², and by March 2022 excavation of about a third of the hill had uncovered 93 burials, 23 of them new that season, with three intact tombs holding glass, bronze, beads and pottery. The 2022 season also produced a pair of dice, the first found in Bahrain, read as part of a game or a fortune-telling ritual of the middle Tylos period (50 BC – 150 AD).
sites.sig: One of more than 30 Tylos cemeteries in the Shakhura–Abu Saiba–Maqaba area, and the one being excavated with modern methods today.

sites.s: Earliest Christian building in the Gulf · excavated 2019–23
sites.se: Under a cemetery mound in Muharraq lay an eight-room building with plaster crosses, perhaps the residence of the bishop of Mashmahig
sites.sa: تحت تل مقبرة في المحرق مبنى من ثماني غرف بصلبان جصية، ربما كان مقر أسقف مشماهيج
sites.desc: Found under a mound in the village cemetery of Samahij on Muharraq, beneath a later mosque that helped preserve it. Excavated from 2019 to 2023 by Timothy Insoll of the University of Exeter and Salman Almahari of the Bahrain Authority for Culture and Antiquities, the stone building has plastered walls and floors and eight surviving rooms, including a kitchen with hearths made from amphora bases, a refectory, a workroom and three living rooms. Radiocarbon dates place its use between the mid-4th and mid-8th centuries AD, after which it was abandoned as the population became Muslim. Finds include three plaster crosses, graffiti of a fish and part of a Chi-Rho, about a dozen copper coins probably Sasanian, carnelian beads and Indian pottery, small wine glasses, spindle whorls and copper needles, and remains of pork, fish and shellfish. It may have been the residence of the bishop of the diocese recorded as Meshmahig in Church of the East sources, which mention a bishop excommunicated in 410.
sites.sig: The first physical evidence of the Church of the East in Bahrain and probably the oldest Christian building known in the Arabian Gulf.

sites.s: Man-made island around a sea spring · National Heritage List
sites.el: Walls enclosing an islet under 20 m, later 40 m wide
sites.te: An island built around a spring
sites.se: Walls and coral platforms built in the sea around a freshwater spring so pearling boats could take on water
sites.sa: جدران ومنصات مرجانية بُنيت في البحر حول عين عذبة ليتزود منها الغواصون بالماء
sites.desc: A small islet north-west of Muharraq, between Busaiteen and Bahrain Bay, long thought natural. Excavations from January 2022 by a British team under Robert Carter with the Bahrain Authority for Culture and Antiquities, the first systematic marine and underwater archaeology survey in Bahrain, showed it was built in the sea around a freshwater spring of the kind local people call a kawkab or chochab. A circular wall enclosed a cistern around the spring, forming an island under 20 m wide; a later curved wall widened it to about 40 m, straight walls enclosed rectangular cabins, and large coral blocks formed a platform more than 60 m long, with a small building holding a water-raising mechanism beside the spring. Pottery of the 7th–8th centuries AD lies mixed with piles of pearl oysters that cover most of the island, and water was drawn for boats anchored along the quay. Threatened by a road project in 2022, it was placed on the National Heritage List.
sites.sig: Described by Salman Al-Mahari as one of the oldest examples of sea filling anywhere, and a direct link between the island's sea springs and its pearling fleet.

sites.se: Chalky dolostone with chert nodules and geodes, laid down in lagoons and tidal channels of a narrow Eocene strait
sites.sa: دولوستون طباشيري بعقد الصوان والجيودات، ترسب في بحيرات ساحلية وقنوات مدّية لمضيق إيوسيني ضيق
sites.desc: An outcrop of about 1.6 km² at the Horse Racing Club in central Bahrain, on the northern edge of the doubly plunging anticline, where a 26.5 m section of the Rus Formation is exposed; boreholes show the formation thickens to about 125 m in the west and 73 m in the east of the island. A 2023 study by Aimen Amer and colleagues logged 13 facies of dolostone, dolomitic marl and claystone with chert nodules near the top and calcite geodes in several beds; XRD showed 88% of 58 samples to be mainly dolomite, and only quartz pseudomorphs after gypsum and thin halite laminae remain of the evaporites. The beds record restricted lagoons, sabkha pools, tidal flats and channels and storm washovers along a shoreline trending NNW–SSE, with wind-blown quartz sand probably from the Arabian Shield. The authors argue that the Rus here is not mainly evaporitic and question its role as a regional hydrocarbon seal.
sites.sig: The most detailed published section of the Rus Formation in Bahrain, the unit that holds the island's lowest aquifer and the geodes found across the interior.

Rock blocks are believed to have been cut here and carried across the water to build the Barbar temple on the north coast of Bahrain Island, whose second temple was walled with carved quarried stone. The island is joined to Umm an Nasan by a 1.75 km causeway, is uninhabited and is closed to the public.

sites.n: Pleistocene Shelf of the King Fahd Causeway
sites.na: رصيف البليستوسين عند جسر الملك فهد
sites.s: Ice-age sea-level record under the causeway
sites.el: Dolomite up to 40 m · cover 3–9 m
sites.se: Boreholes for the causeway cut through dolomite and sands recording the emptying and refilling of the Arabian Gulf
sites.sa: اخترقت حفريات الجسر دولوميت ورمالًا تسجل جفاف الخليج العربي وامتلاءه من جديد
sites.desc: Sediments studied along the King Fahd Causeway between Bahrain and Saudi Arabia by Ata Darwish and Curtis Conley (1990). A lower dolomite interval up to 40 m thick is built of repeated cycles of skeletal packstone, mudstone, pelletal grainstone and green mudstone, dated to the mid-Pleistocene before the first great sea-level fall of 110,000–90,000 years ago. Above it a 3–9 m interval of quartz sandstone, skeletal grainstone, quartz sand and aragonitic oolitic sand records a transgression of 90,000–75,000 years ago, a late Pleistocene blanket of dune sand as aridity grew, and the Flandrian flooding of the Gulf about 6,000 years ago. During the lowstand the whole Gulf was emptied and the sediments were leached, cemented and dolomitised; in wetter periods fresh water dissolved aragonite and precipitated calcite.
sites.sig: A measured record of how the shallow Gulf floor between Bahrain and Arabia dried out and flooded with the ice ages.

sites.se: A low island off the south-east coast whose seagrass beds feed dugongs and turtles and shelter young shrimp and fish

Its sandy beaches are ringed by extensive seagrass beds and reefs; the seagrass is an important feeding area for dugongs and sea turtles and a protected nursery ground for shrimp and finfish, and the island is also recognised as an Important Bird Area. Bahrain's seagrass comprises three species, Halodule uninervis, Halophila stipulacea and Halophila ovalis, with the largest beds running from south of Fasht al-Adhm to the Hawar Islands.

sites.se: A sheltered mudflat bay on Muharraq where mangroves have been replanted for waders and young fish

It was declared a marine protected area in 2003 by Order No. 4 of the Public Commission for the Protection of Marine Resources, Environment and Wildlife, as a site for mangrove restoration and wildlife habitat, and a mangrove reserve has been planted on its north-east shore. The bay is an important resting and feeding area for resident and migratory waders and shelters juvenile fish; the greater flamingo is present year-round on Bahrain's tidal flats. Bahrain's only natural mangrove stand, of Avicennia marina, survives at Tubli Bay, which makes the Arad planting the island's second mangrove site.

sites.te: The grey bird of the palm groves
sites.se: An abandoned palm garden near Budaiya where Bahrain's wintering grey hypocolius gather to roost

Scattered date palms cover about 60% of it. BirdLife International identified it as an Important Bird Area, last assessed in 1994, as the main roost in Bahrain of the grey hypocolius (Hypocolius ampelinus), a passage and wintering bird that feeds by day in palm gardens elsewhere on the island. It has no legal protection, though it has been proposed as a wildlife reserve, and faces cutting of palm scrub, disturbance of the roosts, rubbish and encroaching housing.

sites.desc: Manama lies on the northern coast of Bahrain’s main island; Bahrain’s harbour moved here in the 19th century from Qal’at al-Bahrain. By 1904 the town had more than 450 shops in its souqs, including Souq al-Ajam and Souq al-Yahud, and the region’s first municipal government was set up here in 1919. More than 120 places of worship of four religions stand in the town, among them the Sri Krishna Temple, Bahrain’s largest Hindu temple, a synagogue, mosques and three main churches. The National Heritage Register includes 31 houses in Manama.
sites.sig: A historic Gulf trading town where communities of different faiths have lived side by side.

sites.desc: Awali, in Bahrain’s Southern Governorate, has been built since 1934 by the Bahrain Petroleum Company (Bapco) as a settlement of about 400 buildings, mostly from the 1930s and 1940s with upgrades in the 1950s. Its layout follows the European garden city and garden suburb movements, with houses around a central green and offices in a central location. Housing ranges from bunkhouses for male workers to family houses and small villas, most with private gardens. The UNESCO entry notes the region’s first central sewage system and the world’s first centralized air-conditioning system for an entire settlement.
sites.sig: An early planned oil town that records the start of the oil industry in the Arabian Peninsula.

sites.desc: Hayr Bu ‘Amamah is one of the three offshore oyster beds of the World Heritage property Pearling, Testimony of an Island Economy, inscribed in 2012, with an inscribed area of 4,854.77 ha about 57 km from mainland Bahrain. A hayr is a flat rocky seabed deeper than 10 m dominated by pearl oyster beds. A 2025 survey at 15.9–16.9 m found up to 47 oysters per m², with Pinctada radiata making up 81.3% of the bivalve community at one site, and the study’s highest pearl incidence (14.3%) at the other. It was declared a marine protected area by Supreme Council for Environment Resolution No. 3 of 2017.

It was first declared a marine protected area in 2007 and is now protected under Supreme Council for Environment Resolution No. 3 of 2017. A 2025 survey at 16.2–20.6 m depth found coarse sand over bedrock with up to 30 oysters per m² and the largest oysters in the study, up to 8.2 cm.

sites.desc: Hayr Shtayyah is the largest of the three offshore oyster beds of the World Heritage property Pearling, Testimony of an Island Economy, inscribed in 2012, with an inscribed area of 24,569.6 ha about 30 km from mainland Bahrain. A 2025 survey at 10.9–12.1 m depth found 54–67 oysters per m², the highest proportions of young oysters (spat) in the study at 41.9% and 55%, and hard coral cover of 22.6% at one site. It had the highest biodiversity of the northern sites, with hard and soft corals, sponges and anemones. It was declared a marine protected area by Supreme Council for Environment Resolution No. 3 of 2017.
